judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'You will be expected to contribute' is not plainly a binding obligation, and the amount is left to be 'determined after a consultation with your Branch manager, Regional President and/or Private Chent Group Management and pursuant to applicable legal considerations' — no formula, no cap, and 'and/or' leaves the decision-maker uncertain. Both the existence and the quantum of the duty are genuinely indefinite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 13(c) (which treats the contribution as a compensation adjustment, implying it is mandatory) and Paragraph 15 (which refers to surviving 'indemnification obligations' that appear nowhere else in the instrument by that name): the surrounding text assumes a firm obligation this clause only 'expects'. That mismatch is a live cross-provision problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The obligations are stated flatly (responsibility for errors, no profits from covering errors, no 'trading' in an error account), and the one soft phrase — 'subject to disciplinary action' — is expressly limited by applicable law. Little that two sides could read differently.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 13(c) (errors adjust Net Eligible Revenue) and Paragraph 9(a) (final compensation adjustments): the treatment is consistent across the compensation provisions. No competing allocation of error liability appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Net Eligible Revenue' is capitalised as a defined term but is defined nowhere in the Agreement, and 'yadgment' is a mechanical error; the promissory-note parenthetical ('charges spread beyond three (3) months') is a definition-by-example of uncertain reach. The undefined key term is the nameable defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 3, which incorporates the New FA Compensation Plan 'as that Plan may be modified from tme to ime': the missing definition lives in an extrinsic, unilaterally amendable document, so the size of the adjustment is set outside the instrument. That dependency is a genuine but common structural feature rather than a flat contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The disclosures describe an obligation to arbitrate disputes 'between you and Wells Fargo Advisors, or a client, or any other person', then carve out State unemployment insurance claims by an enumerated parenthetical that mixes unemployment, workers' compensation and NLRA claims, and add a further exclusion for benefit-plan administrative procedures — the boundaries of the carve-outs are contestable and 'the arbitration forum in the claim is filed' is a mechanical error. The EEOC passage also purports to convert an administratively exhausted claim into an arbitrable one, which is a nameable ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 14(b), which by its terms covers only disputes 'arising between you and Wells Fargo Advisors' — narrower than 14(a)'s 'or a client, or any other person' — and against 14(c), which reserves court access for the employer only; the scope described in the disclosures does not match the operative clause. That is a specific, named conflict between an explanatory recital-like passage and the operative arbitration term.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The covered-claims list ends with 'federal, state or local statute or ordinance and/or other theory', an open catch-all after specifics whose reach must be construed, and the fallback designates 'the American Arbitration Association pursuant to its Securities Arbitration Rules, effective May 1, 1993' — a rule set whose current existence and content are uncertain. The FINRA-declines trigger ('does not accept ... or any portion thereof') also invites argument about when it operates.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 14(a) (broader scope, including clients and 'any other person'), 14(c) (employer may go to court notwithstanding any other provision) and Paragraph 7 (at-will employment, which under the Missouri law chosen in Paragraph 16 bears on whether the arbitration promise is illusory): the mutuality and scope of this clause cannot be settled without reading it against those provisions. This is the clause most likely to have been placed before a court.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It is a one-sided carve-out — only Wells Fargo may go to court, and only to enforce Paragraphs 11 and 12 — opening with 'Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement'; the asymmetry is the kind of drafting a court construes against the drafter if any genuine ambiguity appears. It also does not say whether court relief is interim or final, or what happens to the merits.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 14(a), which tells the employee she is 'giving up the right to sue Wells Fargo Advisors ... in court concerning matters related to or arising from your employment', and 14(b), which makes arbitration exclusive: 14(c) reserves the courts for the employer alone, and notably omits Paragraph 10(b)(ii)(A)'s de facto non-compete from what may be enjoined. The asymmetry and the omission are both concrete cross-provision points.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The survival list is 'including, but not limited to, the confidentiality provisions, post-employment restrictions and indemnification obligations', a catch-all over specifics, and it names 'indemnification obligations' that no paragraph of the Agreement actually creates under that label. The assignment terms are one-directional but clearly stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 20, which contains its own, differently worded survival rule (provisions that 'require survival ... in order to give full legal effect'), and Paragraph 13(a), the only candidate for an 'indemnification obligation': two survival clauses with different tests, one referring to an obligation not created elsewhere, is a real incoherence. Reconcilable, but a court would have something to work on.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence choice-of-law clause naming a single state and expressly excluding renvoi; there is no term in it with a second reasonable meaning. Its brevity is a virtue here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 1 (New York branch), Paragraph 12 (restrictive covenants) and Paragraph 14 (arbitration): Missouri law governing covenants performed in New York can raise a public-policy override, and under Missouri law the at-will provision in Paragraph 7 bears on consideration for the arbitration promise. The clause itself does not contradict anything, but its interaction with those provisions is not trivial.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The reformation-then-severance structure is a standard two-step and is stated clearly, though 'the invalidity or unenforceability of any Provision ... shall not affect the validity or unenforceability of the remaining Provisions' is an evident slip (it should read 'enforceability'), which literally read says the opposite of what is intended. That mechanical error is nameable and goes to meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 12 and Paragraph 10(b)(ii)(A) (the restraints most likely to be attacked) and Paragraph 17's own captions sentence: the clause is designed to operate on those and does not contradict them. No conflicting provision found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, conventional non-waiver clause; 'forgo enforcement of a breach ... on an individual matter or matters' is slightly loose but carries only one sensible reading. Nothing to name as ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 8 (no modification except by signed writing) and Paragraph 20 (entire agreement): the non-waiver clause reinforces rather than contradicts them. It is expressed only in the employer's favour, but that asymmetry creates no inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is an acknowledgment, not an operative covenant, and its terms ('read and reviewed', 'opportunity to consult with an attorney') are factual recitals with little to construe. The heading 'RESTRICTIVE COVENANTS' promises substance the paragraph does not contain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 17, which says captions 'shall not affect in any way the meaning or interpretation of this Agreement', and Paragraphs 11, 12 and 10(b)(ii)(A), which contain the actual restraints: the mismatch between heading and content is neutralised by the captions clause. Little cross-provision risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Regarding the matters addressed herein' qualifies the integration in a way whose boundary is uncertain, and the survival test — provisions that 'require survival ... in order to give full legal effect thereto' — is circular and identifies no particular provisions. Both are nameable indefiniteness in a clause meant to be definitive.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Paragraph 8 ('This Agreement serves only as a synopsis of the compensation and other arrangements'), Paragraph 6 (the Agreement 'does not supersede or replace' Wells Fargo HR and compliance policies) and Paragraph 15 (a differently worded survival clause): a document that is only a synopsis and expressly subordinate to outside policies cannot easily be the entire understanding, and two survival tests coexist. These are specific, named conflicts.
